s.line: The four travelers passed through the rest of the forest in safety,
s.note: בְּשָׁלוֹם "in peace" = safely, unharmed: הֵם הִגִּיעוּ הַבַּיְתָה בְּשָׁלוֹם (they got home safe). אַרְבַּעַת is the construct form of אַרְבָּעָה: "the four (of)" before a definite noun.

w: וּכְשֶׁיָּצְאוּ|and when they came out|pa'al · י־צ־א
s.line: and when they came out from its gloom saw before them a steep hill, covered from top to bottom with great pieces of rock.
s.note: מְכֻסָּה (covered) is a pu'al participle; the active pi'el is כִּסָּה (to cover). מְכֻסֶּה בְּ… = covered with …. Compare כִּסּוּי (a lid, a cover).

s.line: “That will be a hard climb,” said the Scarecrow, “but we must get over the hill, nevertheless.”
s.note: בְּכָל זֹאת = "nevertheless, anyway, all the same", very common in speech: הָיָה קַר, אֲבָל יָצָאנוּ בְּכָל זֹאת. טִפּוּס (a climb) is the noun of טִפֵּס (pi'el, to climb).

s.line: So he led the way and the others followed.
They had nearly reached the first rock when they heard a rough voice cry out, “Keep back!”
s.note: הִתְרַחֵק (hitpa'el) = to move away, keep one's distance, from רָחוֹק (far). Its opposite is הִתְקָרֵב (to come closer), from קָרוֹב. Both take מִ־ / אֶל: הִתְרַחֵק מֵהַכְּבִישׁ!

s.line: “Who are you?” asked the Scarecrow.
Then a head showed itself over the rock and the same voice said,
s.note: הוֹפִיעַ (hif'il) = to appear, show up; also "to perform, appear on stage": הַזַּמֶּרֶת תּוֹפִיעַ הָעֶרֶב. The noun הוֹפָעָה = a show, a concert.

s.line: “This hill belongs to us, and we don’t allow anyone to cross it.”
s.note: מַרְשֶׁה לְ… = allows (someone) to …; the person gets לְ. The noun רְשׁוּת (permission) and רִשְׁיוֹן (a license) are from the same root. שַׁיָּךְ לְ… = belongs to.

s.line: “But we must cross it,” said the Scarecrow.
“We’re going to the country of the Quadlings.”
s.note: בַּדֶּרֶךְ לְ… = "on the way to …", the natural Hebrew for "we're going to". On the phone you'll hear אֲנִי בַּדֶּרֶךְ = I'm on my way.

s.line: “But you shall not!” replied the voice,
s.note: הֵשִׁיב (hif'il of שָׁב, to return) = to reply, "send back" an answer; a little more literary than עָנָה. תְּשׁוּבָה (answer) is from the same root.

s.line: and there stepped from behind the rock the strangest man the travelers had ever seen.
s.note: אֵי פַּעַם = "ever" (at any time): הָיִיתָ אֵי פַּעַם בְּאֵילַת? (have you ever been to Eilat?). With לֹא you usually say אַף פַּעַם לֹא instead.

w: וְהָיָה לוֹ|and he had|~lit. there was to him
s.line: He was quite short and stout and had a big head, which was flat at the top and supported by a thick neck full of wrinkles.
s.note: נִתְמַךְ is nif'al used as the passive of תָּמַךְ (to support): "was supported". תְּמִיכָה = support, a word you'll meet in the news (תְּמִיכָה בַּמֶּמְשָׁלָה) and in tech help: תְּמִיכָה טֶכְנִית. לְמַדַּי = fairly, quite.

w: הָיוּ לוֹ|he had|~lit. there were to him
s.line: But he had no arms at all,
s.note: יָד covers the whole arm and the hand; זְרוֹעַ is the arm specifically. Putting יָדַיִם first stresses it: "arms, he had none at all".

s.line: and, seeing this, the Scarecrow did not fear that so helpless a creature could prevent them from climbing the hill.
s.note: חֲסַר אוֹנִים = helpless, a fixed phrase (אוֹנִים = strength). מָנַע מִ… = prevented (someone) from …: the person gets מִ־, the action is an infinitive. חָשַׁשׁ = to fear, worry, a little more formal than פָּחַד.

w: מוֹצֵא חֵן בְּעֵינֶיךָ|pleases you|~idiom: finds favor in your eyes
s.line: So he said, “I’m sorry not to do as you wish, but we must pass over your hill whether you like it or not,”
s.note: מִצְטַעֵר (hitpa'el of צ־ע־ר) = sorry; the ת of hitpa'el swaps to ט after צ. מוֹצֵא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי… = "is pleasing to …", the everyday way to say "like": הַסֶּרֶט מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינַי (I liked the film). בֵּין אִם … וּבֵין אִם לֹא = whether … or not.

s.line: and he walked boldly forward.

As quick as lightning the man’s head shot forward and his neck stretched out until the top of the head, where it was flat, struck the Scarecrow in the middle and sent him tumbling, over and over, down the hill.
s.note: זִנֵּק (pi'el) = to leap, shoot forward; זִנּוּק is the start of a race, and in the news prices זִנְּקוּ = soared. נִמְתַּח = stretched (itself); מֶתַח = tension, suspense, and סֶרֶט מֶתַח is a thriller.

w: שׁוּב וָשׁוּב|over and over|~lit. again and again
s.note: פָּגַע בְּ… = to hit, strike; also to hurt someone's feelings: הוּא פָּגַע בִּי. הִתְגַּלְגֵּל = to roll (along), from גַּלְגַּל (a wheel). בְּמוֹרַד = down (a slope); the opposite is בְּמַעֲלֶה = up.

s.line: Almost as quickly as it came the head went back to the body,
and the man laughed harshly as he said, “It isn’t as easy as you think!”
s.note: צָחַק צְחוֹק צוֹרֵם: verb + noun from the same root, with an adjective, as in קָד קִידָה. צוֹרֵם = harsh, grating (of a sound), and figuratively "jarring": זֶה צוֹרֵם לִי (that grates on me).

s.line: A chorus of boisterous laughter came from the other rocks,
s.note: נִשְׁמַע = was heard (nif'al of שָׁמַע). Its everyday use: מָה נִשְׁמָע? = "what's new? how are you?", literally "what is heard?". זֶה נִשְׁמָע טוֹב = that sounds good.

s.line: and Dorothy saw hundreds of the armless Hammer-Heads upon the hillside, one behind every rock.
s.note: חַסְרֵי is the plural construct of חֲסַר (lacking): חֲסַר בַּיִת = homeless, חֲסַר סַבְלָנוּת = impatient. A handy way to make "-less" words.

s.line: The Lion became quite angry at the laughter caused by the Scarecrow’s mishap,
s.note: תַּקָּלָה = a mishap, a hitch; today mostly a technical fault: תַּקָּלָה בַּמַּחְשֵׁב. עוֹרֵר = to arouse, stir up (עוֹרֵר סַקְרָנוּת, aroused curiosity); שָׁעוֹן מְעוֹרֵר is an alarm clock.

s.line: and giving a loud roar that echoed like thunder, he dashed up the hill.
s.note: הִסְתָּעֵר (hitpa'el) = to charge, storm, from סְעָרָה (a storm); the ת swaps places with the ס. הִדְהֵד = to echo; הֵד = an echo.

s.line: Again a head shot swiftly out,
and the great Lion went rolling down the hill as if he had been struck by a cannon ball.
s.note: English "as if he had been struck by a cannon ball" becomes active in Hebrew: "as if a cannon ball had hit him". כְּאִלּוּ = as if; in slang it is also a filler word like "like": הוּא כְּאִלּוּ לֹא שָׁמַע.

s.line: Dorothy ran down and helped the Scarecrow to his feet,
s.note: עָזַר לְ…: in Hebrew you help to someone (לַדַּחְלִיל), never with אֶת. רָצָה here is "she ran" (ר־ו־ץ); without vowels רצה can also be רָצָה "he wanted" (ר־צ־ה). Context decides.

w: כּוֹאֵב לוֹ|hurting him|~lit. hurts to him
אֵין טַעַם|it is useless|~lit. there is no sense
s.line: and the Lion came up to her, feeling rather bruised and sore, and said, “It is useless to fight people with shooting heads;
s.note: כּוֹאֵב לִי = "it hurts me, I'm in pain": the person in pain gets לְ, the body part is the subject: כּוֹאֵב לִי הָרֹאשׁ (I have a headache). אֵין טַעַם + infinitive = "there's no point in …". נוֹרִים is the nif'al (passive) of יָרָה (to shoot): נוֹרוּ יְרִיּוֹת = shots were fired, a common news phrase.

w: לַעֲמֹד בִּפְנֵיהֶם|withstand them|~idiom: stand before them
s.line: no one can withstand them.”
s.note: לַעֲמֹד בִּפְנֵי = to withstand, hold out against: לֹא יָכֹלְתִּי לַעֲמֹד בִּפְנֵי הַפִּתּוּי (I couldn't resist the temptation). עָמַד בְּ… has a related use: עָמַד בַּלַּחַץ = withstood the pressure.

s.line: “What can we do, then?” she asked.
“Call the Winged Monkeys,” suggested the Tin Woodman.
s.note: תִּקְרְאִי is future tense used as a polite request; in speech it is softer than the imperative קִרְאִי. קָרָא לְ… = to call (someone); קָרָא alone, or with אֶת, = to read.

w: יֵשׁ לָךְ|you have|~lit. there is to you
s.line: “You have still the right to command them once more.”
s.note: זְכוּת = a right; זְכֻיּוֹת אָדָם = human rights, and יֵשׁ לְךָ זְכוּת לִשְׁתֹּק = you have the right to remain silent. עוֹד פַּעַם אַחַת = one more time.

s.line: “Very well,” she answered,
and putting on the Golden Cap she uttered the magic words.
s.note: חָבַשׁ is the verb for putting on a hat or helmet (חָבַשׁ קַסְדָּה); for clothes it is לָבַשׁ, for shoes נָעַל. חָבַשׁ also means to bandage: a medic is a חוֹבֵשׁ.

s.line: The Monkeys were as prompt as ever, and in a few moments the entire band stood before her.
s.note: סְפוּרִים = "a few", literally "counted": so few you can count them (סָפַר = to count). תּוֹךְ דַּקּוֹת סְפוּרוֹת (within minutes) is a favorite news phrase.

s.line: “What are your commands?” inquired the King of the Monkeys, bowing low.
“Carry us over the hill to the country of the Quadlings,” answered the girl.
s.note: נָשָׂא = to carry, a bit more literary than סָחַב. Its nun drops out in the future (תִּשְׂאוּ). Modern uses: נָשָׂא נְאוּם = gave a speech, נוֹשֵׂא = a topic, subject.

s.line: “It shall be done,” said the King,
s.note: יֵעָשֶׂה = will be done, the nif'al (passive) of עָשָׂה. You'll hear the past נַעֲשָׂה constantly: מָה נַעֲשָׂה? = what's been done?, and נַעֲשָׂה מְאֻחָר = it's getting late.

s.line: and at once the Winged Monkeys caught the four travelers and Toto up in their arms and flew away with them.
As they passed over the hill the Hammer-Heads yelled with vexation, and shot their heads high in the air,
s.note: שִׁלַּח (pi'el) = to send off, launch, let fly; compare pa'al שָׁלַח = to send (שָׁלַחְתִּי לְךָ הוֹדָעָה, I sent you a message). The pi'el is stronger and more forceful.

s.line: but they could not reach the Winged Monkeys, which carried Dorothy and her comrades safely over the hill and set them down in the beautiful country of the Quadlings.
s.note: הִצְלִיחַ + infinitive = to manage to, succeed in; "could not" after an attempt is usually לֹא הִצְלִיחַ rather than לֹא יָכֹל. הוֹרִיד (hif'il of יָרַד) = to bring down, set down; a taxi מוֹרִיד you at your stop. Note the adjective הַיָּפָה at the end: it describes אֶרֶץ (feminine), not the Quadlings.

s.line: “This is the last time you can summon us,” said the leader to Dorothy;
s.note: זִמֵּן (pi'el) = to summon, call in: זֻמַּן לַחֲקִירָה = was summoned for questioning (pu'al), a common news phrase. הִזְמִין (hif'il, same root) = to invite or to order: הִזְמַנְתִּי פִּיצָה.

s.line: “so good-bye and good luck to you.”
s.note: בְּהַצְלָחָה! = good luck!, said before an exam, a trip, a new job. It comes from הִצְלִיחַ (to succeed), the verb you just saw.

s.line: “Good-bye, and thank you very much,” returned the girl;

w: וּכְהֶרֶף עַיִן|and in a twinkling|~idiom: like a blink of an eye
s.line: and the Monkeys rose into the air and were out of sight in a twinkling.
s.note: כְּהֶרֶף עַיִן = in the blink of an eye. נֶעֱלַם (nif'al) = to disappear, with an active meaning; נֶעְדָּר is the word for a missing person. הִתְרוֹמֵם = to rise up; הֵרִים (above) = to lift something.

s.line: The country of the Quadlings seemed rich and happy.
s.note: אֶרֶץ is feminine, so the verb and adjectives are feminine too: נִרְאֲתָה עֲשִׁירָה וּמְאֻשֶּׁרֶת.

s.line: There was field upon field of ripening grain, with well-paved roads running between,
s.note: סָלוּל (paved) is the pa'ul participle of סָלַל (to pave a road). מְסִלָּה (a track, a route) is from the same root; מְסִלַּת בַּרְזֶל = a railway. דֶּרֶךְ is usually feminine, so סְלוּלוֹת. הִבְשִׁיל (hif'il) = to ripen, from בָּשֵׁל (ripe).

s.line: and pretty rippling brooks with strong bridges across them.
s.note: פֶּלֶג = a brook, stream; today it also means a faction of a party: פֶּלֶג בַּמִּפְלָגָה. מִפְלָגָה (a political party) and הִפְלִיג (to sail) share the root. מְפַכֶּה is a literary word for the sound of a babbling brook.

s.line: The fences and houses and bridges were all painted bright red, just as they had been painted yellow in the country of the Winkies and blue in the country of the Munchkins.
s.note: עַז = strong, intense: for colors it means "bright, vivid" (אָדֹם עַז); for coffee or a smell, "strong". The dash before בְּכָחֹל stands for the repeated words הֵם הָיוּ צְבוּעִים, a common way to avoid repeating a verb.

w: וְטוֹבֵי לֵב|and good-natured|~lit. good of heart
s.line: The Quadlings themselves, who were short and fat and looked chubby and good-natured, were dressed all in red,
s.note: עַצְמָם = themselves, after a noun for emphasis: הַמּוֹרִים עַצְמָם (the teachers themselves). טוֹב לֵב = kind-hearted, good-natured; plural טוֹבֵי לֵב. עֲגַלְגַּל = roundish, chubby, from עָגֹל (round), with the repeated syllable softening it, as in יְרַקְרַק (greenish).

w: עַל רֶקַע|against|~lit. on the background of
s.line: which showed bright against the green grass and the yellowing grain.
s.note: בָּלַט עַל רֶקַע … = stood out against …; בּוֹלֵט = prominent, conspicuous. עַל רֶקַע is also a news phrase meaning "against the background of, amid": עַל רֶקַע הַמַּשְׁבֵּר (amid the crisis). Hif'il color verbs like הִצְהִיב mean "to turn (a color)": הֶאְדִּים = to blush, turn red.

s.line: The Monkeys had set them down near a farmhouse, and the four travelers walked up to it and knocked at the door.
s.note: דָּפַק בַּדֶּלֶת = knocked on the door, with בְּ־. In slang דָּפַק also means "to cheat, screw over": דָּפְקוּ אוֹתִי = I got ripped off. נִגַּשׁ אֶל = to approach; נָגִישׁ = accessible.

s.line: It was opened by the farmer’s wife,
s.note: English "it was opened by the farmer's wife" becomes active in Hebrew: "the farmer's wife opened it". A passive with "by" (<t>נִפְתְּחָה עַל יְדֵי</t>) exists but sounds formal and official.

s.line: and when Dorothy asked for something to eat the woman gave them all a good dinner, with three kinds of cake and four kinds of cookies, and a bowl of milk for Toto.
s.note: שְׁלוֹשָׁה סוּגֵי עוּגוֹת: the number agrees with סוּג (masculine), not with עוּגוֹת. סוּגֵי is the construct plural. עוּגִיָּה (cookie) is a diminutive of עוּגָה (cake), with the ending ־יָּה.

s.line: “How far is it to the Castle of Glinda?” asked the child.
s.note: כַּמָּה רָחוֹק? = how far?, and likewise כַּמָּה זְמַן? (how long?), כַּמָּה זֶה עוֹלֶה? (how much does it cost?). כַּמָּה is the all-purpose "how much / how many".

s.line: “It is not a great way,” answered the farmer’s wife.
s.note: אֵשֶׁת הַחַקְלַאי is the construct form of אִשָּׁה; it means the same as אִשְׁתּוֹ שֶׁל הַחַקְלַאי above.

s.line: “Take the road to the South and you will soon reach it.”
s.note: דָּרוֹמָה = southward: the ending ־ָה marks direction "to": צָפוֹנָה (north), הַבַּיְתָה (home), הַחוּצָה (outside). אֵלֶיהָ refers to הַטִּירָה, which is feminine.

s.line: Thanking the good woman, they started afresh and walked by the fields and across the pretty bridges until they saw before them a very beautiful Castle.
s.note: הוֹדָה לְ… = to thank someone, with לְ; תּוֹדָה is from the same root. הוֹדָה בְּ… = to admit, confess: הוּא הוֹדָה בָּאַשְׁמָה. יָצָא לַדֶּרֶךְ = set out on the way.
לְאֹרֶךְ = along (לְאֹרֶךְ הַחוֹף, along the beach), from אֹרֶךְ = length. עַל פְּנֵי = across, over the surface of.

s.line: Before the gates were three young girls, dressed in handsome red uniforms trimmed with gold braid;
s.note: מְעֻטָּר (decorated, trimmed) is a pu'al participle; the pi'el עִטֵּר = to decorate, and עֲטָרָה = a crown. מַדִּים = uniform, always plural: לָבַשׁ מַדִּים (put on a uniform). שָׁלוֹשׁ without ה goes with feminine נְעָרוֹת.

s.line: and as Dorothy approached, one of them said to her:
“Why have you come to the South Country?”
“To see the Good Witch who rules here,” she answered.
“Will you take me to her?”
s.note: תִּקְחִי is the future of לָקַח: the ל drops out, as if the root were נ־ק־ח (אֶקַּח, תִּקַּח, יִקְחוּ). As a question, the future is the normal polite way to ask "will you …?".

s.line: “Let me have your name, and I will ask Glinda if she will receive you.”
s.note: מוּכָן = ready, willing; in form a hof'al participle ("made ready") of the root כ־ו־ן, like הֵכִין (to prepare). מוּכָן לְ… = willing to …. מָה שְׁמֵךְ? (to a woman) / מָה שִׁמְךָ? (to a man) = what's your name?, one of the few places the suffix possessive is fully everyday.

s.line: They told who they were, and the girl soldier went into the Castle.
s.note: חַיֶּלֶת = a woman soldier, the feminine of חַיָּל, a very ordinary word in Israel. מִי הֵם: reported speech keeps the present tense, where English shifts to "who they were".

s.line: After a few moments she came back to say that Dorothy and the others were to be admitted at once.
s.note: מֻזְמָן (invited) is the hof'al participle, the passive of hif'il הִזְמִין (to invite). כַּעֲבֹר + time = "after (a period of time)": כַּעֲבֹר שָׁבוּעַ (a week later), a bit more literary than אַחֲרֵי.
